newsitem.title: USA: Mexico debt plan has no major rating impact-S&P.
newsitem.headline: Mexico debt plan has no major rating impact-S&P.

text.p: Mexico's program to restructure its debt profile by prepaying $6.0 billion in floating rate notes due 2001, will not have a major impact on the country's credit rating, Standard & Poor's said Wednesday.

S&P Director of Sovereign Ratings Lacey Gallagher said that Mexico's move unveiled on Wednesday, in which the country would use proceeds from fresh bonds issues to buy up the 2001 notes, was constructive, but would not have the same significance as earlier debt restructurings.
"It's always good to lengthen your external liability profile," Gallagher said. "But it's just a marginal change on top of what has already happened."

Gallagher said that Mexico had succeeded in making major improvements in its external liablities in 1995 and 1996, when it retired its massive short term debt instruments and then transformed its borrowings from the U.S. Treasury into market instruments.
"Now all they are doing is refining the profile of their market debt," Gallagher said. "This is continuing the same strategy, which is very sound, but it's not a milestone."
S&P rates Mexico's long-term foreign currency obligations at BB with a stable outlook.
"It's a BB credit, with a stable outlook. I don't expect any reversal but I also couldn't forecast the speed of progress."
Gallagher said that S&P would be needed to see a longer track record of economic growth and political liberalization to raise its rating.
"There isn't enough of a growth track record to make us confident that Mexico can move into an expansion that other countries of its income level have been able to achieve," she said.
